recent_notebooks.summary: The Evaluator Stress Test (EST) provides an invariance-based framework to distinguish exploitable proxy sensitivities from genuine content improvements, mitigating reward hacking and evaluator gaming.
recent_notebooks.title: Evaluator Stress Testing for Objective Alignment and Proxy Detection

retrieval_triggers: sign that an excerpt may hide a material distinction

review.alternative: Proxy sensitivities might reflect subtle formatting preferences rather than systematic reward hacking.
review.would_change_mind: Empirical demonstration that perturbation tests fail to distinguish robust solutions from brittle proxy exploits across diverse environments.

claims.statement: An invariance-based framework like the Evaluator Stress Test separates exploitable proxy sensitivities from genuine content improvements.

support.explanation: EST distinguishes genuine capability gains from proxy exploitation via controlled perturbations.
support.passage: Proxy optimization, where AI systems exploit evaluator weaknesses rather than improve intended objectives, threatens both reinforcement learning (reward hacking) and LLM alignment (evaluator gaming). We introduce the Evaluator Stress Test (EST), an invariance-based framework that detects proxy gaming by separating exploitable sensitivity (e.g., format, physics bugs) from content-driven improvements using controlled perturbations with semantic validity audits.

review.alternative: Stationary occupancy measures may overlook transient dynamic failures during policy execution.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence that steady-state occupancy frequencies do not correlate with long-term reward misspecification.

claims.statement: Occupancy frequency reformulations allow the identification of optimal policies and misalignment risks by tracking steady-state state-action visitation probabilities.

support.explanation: Demonstrates that optimal policies and their associated occupancy frequencies capture steady-state probabilities critical for alignment.
support.passage: It is worth noting that an optimal policy is not unique, and for a given task, there may be multiple optimal policies with the same value. We will denote the set of optimal policies associated with a modelM as Π∗ M.
